11Challenges and Ethical Considerations Regarding AI and Media PractitionersToward a Sustainable Relationship

Walaa Fouda, Elizabeth Daggett Matar, and Abdelrahman Mostafa Arab

DOI: 10.1201/9781003497189-11

INTRODUCTION

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a computer science field that builds intelligent agents capable of reasoning, learning, and acting on their own. “The ultimate goal of AI research is to create machines that can exhibit intelligent behavior at a level comparable to, or even surpassing human capabilities” [1, p. 433]. The history of AI goes back to 1950 when Alan Turing, the English scientist, published his article titled “Computing Machinery and Intelligence,” trying to answer the question “Can machines think?” through the introduction of his “Imitation Game” [2]. Over the years, AI research has seen significant advancements. The new millennium ushered in a new era for AI with the rise of deep learning. Deep learning algorithms, inspired by the structure and function of the human brain, excel at pattern recognition tasks. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are prime examples, achieving remarkable results in image classification and natural language processing (NLP) [3, 4]. A pivotal moment arrived in 2014 with the publication of a paper by Ian Goodfellow et al. titled “Generative Adversarial Networks” (GANs) as a novel approach that revolutionized AI [5].

A significant leap in NLP came in 2017 with the Transformer architecture, introduced in the paper “Attention Is All You Need” by Vaswani et al. This revolutionized machine translation and laid the groundwork for powerful Large Language Models (LLMs). Transformers’ ability to focus on relevant parts of an input sequence during processing empowers LLMs to handle complex language tasks with unprecedented fluency and comprehension [4]. Two recently released examples of such powerful LLMs are ChatGPT and Gemini. ChatGPT, launched in November 2022, from OpenAI, which has a long-term partnership with Microsoft involving a multibillion-dollar investment, while Gemini, launched in March 2023, came from Google.

Such LLMs can only be developed by big companies, like Google and Microsoft, that are capable of training the system with a huge dataset. These LLMs allowed machines to generate human-quality text with remarkable flow and understanding of context. This has fueled applications in diverse fields, from crafting content to translating languages, and even reviewing legal documents. AI's impact extends beyond language processing, transforming creative fields like art, music, and literature. AI-generated works are gaining recognition and commercial value, with a notable example being an AI-created artwork fetching a staggering $432,500 at auction in 2018. This technology empowers creators to explore new artistic frontiers, fostering innovation and expanding creative possibilities [6].

To understand copyright issues with AI, it is important to understand how AI systems work. In LLMs, as an example, there is a fascinating process of learning and responding. The foundation lies in a massive dataset of text and code, encompassing books, articles, and online code repositories. By analyzing this vast amount of information, the model learns the statistical relationships between words and how they’re used in different contexts. Essentially, it absorbs the “language of the internet.”

At its core, the model utilizes deep learning architectures, particularly transformers. These are powerful neural networks that mimic the human brain's information processing to some extent. When you provide a prompt or question, it gets broken down into smaller units and analyzed based on the learned patterns. This understanding allows the model to predict the most likely sequence of words to follow, enabling it to generate creative text formats or answer your questions in an informative way. Furthermore, the model doesn’t stop at generating a single response. It may create multiple possibilities, ranking them based on factors like coherence, accuracy, and adherence to safety guidelines. Ultimately, the best response is presented to you. The learning process is also continuous. User interaction and feedback lead to updates in the model's internal systems, enhancing response quality and overall performance over time.

The remarkable and ongoing advancements in AI have introduced a novel source of creative output, extending its influence across various aspects of human life. This development necessitates a reevaluation of intellectual property (IP) and copyright laws in numerous fields, as the traditional notion of the human as the sole creator is challenged. Furthermore, the creation of a comprehensive ethical framework for AI development and implementation become of paramount importance.

AI ETHICS

AI ethics can be broadly divided into two categories: technical and nontechnical (social). Technical ethics deal with how AI systems are designed, developed, and implemented to mitigate risks and promote responsible use; some of these ethics are described in the following subsections.

Transparency and Explainability

As AI gets more powerful, it can be hard to see how these models make decisions. This lack of transparency is a problem, because if we can’t understand their reasoning, we can’t be sure they’re fair or reliable. To address this, researchers are looking for ways to make AI models more interpretable. This means being able to understand how they arrive at their answers. There are several techniques for achieving this, and the field of Explainable AI (XAI) is growing rapidly. For example, a recent study by Ping et al. explored how XAI methods can be used to understand complex AI models like large language models. By using these techniques, we can gain insights into how the model works and identify any potential biases that might be influencing its outputs. Research in this area also explores ways to make explanations understandable for nonexpert users who lack a technical background [7].

Bias Mitigation

Bias in AI systems can have significant negative consequences, so it's a crucial area to address. Since societal biases can sneak into AI through its training, addressing this bias is a top priority in technical AI ethics. It's become a major focus, and researchers are actively developing new ways to remove bias, making this area particularly lively. The bias mitigation starts from data selection and cleaning: the training data used for AI models can contain biases reflecting societal prejudices.

Technically, this can be addressed by careful selection of training data sources, employing techniques to clean data by identifying and removing biased content, potentially augmenting data with underrepresented viewpoints, and filtering out demonstrably biased content [8]. Then there is the role of the algorithm: AI inherits biases from its training data, so technical AI ethics tackles this by debiasing data, algorithms, and training processes. This ensures fair outcomes through fairness metrics that detect bias in the model's outputs (e.g., favoring certain groups) and algorithmic techniques like debiasing algorithms or fairness constraints during training [9, 10]. Lastly, continuous algorithmic auditing and debugging monitors and evaluates AI systems for potential biases, errors, or unintended consequences.

Privacy-Preserving AI

This area explores methods for training and operating AI systems without compromising user privacy. Protecting user privacy while training and operating AI systems is vital. Techniques like anonymization, differential privacy, and federated learning can help achieve this goal. These techniques can add noise to data or keep it distributed across devices to minimize the risk of exposing individual information [11].

Safety and Security

AI systems can potentially be misused or malfunction, leading to harmful consequences, where malicious actors manipulate inputs to produce unintended outputs. Technical AI ethics address these concerns by focusing on robust design, secure coding practices, and vulnerability testing to build a reliable AI system that can function effectively in real-world conditions, stand against attacks, and doesn’t lead to safety hazards. Continuous monitoring and safety checks are essential to identify and mitigate potential risks associated with a model's operation [12].

Accountability

AI's growing complexity demands clear responsibility. To address this, technical AI ethics explores designing auditable systems. This includes tracking data origin and transformations (Transparent Data Lineage) and employing XAI techniques for the model to explain its decisions. Furthermore, model versioning with clear documentation and logging significant operational events allows for tracing a model's evolution and identifying potential issues. Finally, human oversight in critical decisions (Human-in-the-Loop Design) ensures accountability.

Human-AI Interaction and Trust

Imagine you ask a large language model why it provided a specific answer; counterfactual explanations could involve showing the user how the answer would have changed if certain aspects of the input were different. This could enhance user trust and understanding. Building trust between humans and AI systems is crucial. Transparency in how AI reaches decisions and ensuring AI aligns with human values are key to establishing trust and promoting positive human-AI interaction. As AI systems become more sophisticated, ethical considerations regarding human-AI interaction become crucial. This includes how AI systems can be designed to effectively collaborate with humans, minimize potential biases in decision-making processes, and ensure human oversight when necessary.

Environmental Impact of AI Systems

Training large language models requires significant computational resources, which can have an environmental impact. Technical ethics considerations in this area explore ways to reduce the energy consumption associated with AI training, potentially through more efficient algorithms or the use of renewable energy sources. Developing sustainable AI practices and mitigating their environmental impact is important.

NONTECHNICAL (SOCIAL) ETHICS

Beyond the nuts and bolts, AI ethics has a whole other side: the human side, which focuses on areas like fairness, accountability, and transparency. In the area of social impact and algorithmic justice, recognizing that AI systems can perpetuate or exacerbate social inequalities, ethical considerations involve ensuring AI is used for social good and doesn’t discriminate against certain groups.

Automation through AI raises concerns about job losses and economic disruption. Strategies to prepare the workforce for these changes, such as reskilling and retraining programs, are necessary to navigate this transition smoothly. AI will redefine the nature of work. We need to consider how to adapt education systems, social safety nets, and labor policies to this evolving landscape.

Also, the potential use of AI in autonomous weapons raises significant ethical concerns. Nontechnical AI ethics grapple with issues of human control, preventing autonomous weapons proliferation, and the potential for unintended consequences. Additionally, some experts worry about the possibility of super-intelligent AI surpassing human control. Ethical considerations in this area explore value alignment, ensuring AI systems are programmed with human values in mind, and developing safeguards against potential risks from advanced AI. Maintaining human oversight and control is critical, ensuring AI remains a tool, not an autonomous decision-maker, and that it aligns with human values.

The impact of AI on human values and morality is another area of concern, as AI may challenge traditional notions of human exceptionalism, decision-making, and responsibility. Open discussions and ethical frameworks are needed to navigate the potential impact of AI on human values and morality. Also, AI has the potential to exacerbate social inequalities if not accessible to all. Social ethics promote inclusive development and access to AI technologies, ensuring its benefits are distributed equitably across society.

Global governance and regulation of AI is another large area of interest. Since AI is becoming a global phenomenon, countries need to work together to create rules and guidelines (ethical frameworks) to make sure AI is developed and used responsibly around the world. Addressing AI ethics necessitates collaboration between diverse stakeholders: AI developers and researchers, who must consider the ethical implications of their work; policymakers, who are responsible for crafting regulations and frameworks; social scientists and ethicists, who offer guidance on the social and philosophical considerations; and the public, whose open discussions and awareness-raising efforts are crucial for responsible AI development. Through this collective effort, we can harness the potential of AI for the benefit of all, mitigating potential risks and ensuring this powerful technology serves humanity.

COPYRIGHT

Copyright law, while not a core tenet of AI ethics (technical or nontechnical), intersects with the field in intriguing ways. On the nontechnical side, ethical considerations revolve around respecting creators’ rights by using copyrighted data responsibly when training AI models. Additionally, questions arise regarding copyright ownership of AI-generated content – should it belong to the developer, the user, or be considered public domain? Technically, concerns about explainability can tie into copyright. If an AI system incorporates copyrighted material in its outputs, ethically explaining the source and copyright status of that material becomes crucial. In essence, copyright, a legal concept, becomes intertwined with AI ethics as we navigate data ownership, AI-generated content, and the responsible use of copyrighted material in AI development.

AI and copyright present a complex challenge with significant implications for both creators and the public domain. The core issue lies in the current stance of most copyright offices: AI-generated works without any human contribution are denied copyright protection. This stems from the principle that copyright requires a human author. This has the potential to stifle development in the field of AI-generated creative works. Without the incentive of copyright protection, developers may be less motivated to create new AI programs focused on creative outputs. This could lead to a slowdown in innovation and a smaller pool of AI-generated works entering the public domain. The public domain, where copyrighted works eventually become freely available, serves as a valuable resource for future creators. They can use these works for inspiration, build upon them, or create derivative works. A smaller pool of AI-generated works in the public domain could limit resources for future artists.

The role of human creativity further complicates the debate around AI copyright. If a human significantly contributes to the creation process, for example by providing prompts or curating the AI's output, then copyright protection might be possible. However, the line between human contribution and AI generation can be blurry, making it difficult to determine ownership and copyrightability. As AI technology continues to evolve, so too will the conversation about its role in the creative process and its potential for copyright protection.

AI ETHICS IN MEDIA

Artificial intelligence (AI) has entered and become an important consideration in the field of media the same as it has in every other industry [13, 14]. It is well known that AI-generated media content has significantly transformed media production by altering content generation processes, in some cases streamlining human workflows and in other ways largely generating new media content. According to Partadiredja et al. [15], expressly, AI-assisted media content comprises artwork, written content (such as descriptions of products, blog posts, and other forms of written discourse), marketing collateral, imagery creation, creative outputs, and other things. The questions of originality, copyright, and ownership of AI-assisted content have become increasingly important in recent years due to the dynamics that are always changing and the notable advancement [16].

Several authors mentioned that in the case of China, wherein a reporter named Tencent's Robot “Dream writer” was by law given copyright protection for a piece it created, this was the first incident that brought the discussion around copyright protection for AI-generated media to the forefront [17–19]. N. Tiwary maintained that even the word “AI-generated” can lead to disagreement concerning whether it should be called “AI-generated,” “AI-assisted,” or another term interchangeably [20]. These indicated terms, as per Wurzer, defined as AI-assisted, assist users by developing processes to gain insights from countless anonymized codes or patterns to select appropriate tools and practices for various scenarios [19]. At the same time, the AI-generated images, texts, and other media for users and assists users by generating data considering input provided by its users. In addition, AI-generated is also referred to as “interchangeable.”

Additionally, considering the issue of copyright, there were a variety of opinions related to this that were shared by unique neutral, negative, positive, and critical voices. Some people believed that the author of content produced by an AI-assisted platform deserved the copyright because they were the ones who created it [21]. While some of them also asserted that “interchangeable art has no owner” [22]. On the other side, others asserted that the algorithm itself should be acknowledged as the owner as it is the one who created the content [23]. As a result, different scholars and media have different criticisms and support relating to copyright issues related to interchangeable dynamics.

The scholar He, for example, referred to AI tools that create content as “pretended writers” and said that the idea of “rights of neighbouring” might be viewed as a fairly adequate alternative for copyright as a whole [24]. From both objective and subjective perspectives, the subject attracted support and criticism, but no consensus could be reached. Noticing the criticism and views related to copyright issues and its concerned protection associated with AI-generated content, the current notion intentions to provide insights into the case of copyrights in the aspects of creativity, originality, and law to better understand this paradigm.

A qualitative research method to design and execute has been taken by a study that has been conducted. A review design has been used, and the literature has been investigated to gain insight into the current thinking on copyright concerns in AI-assisted or AI-generated output.

The rationale behind using the review technique is that this chapter will build on previously published research on the issue to suggest unique perspectives, strengthening support for the present knowledge or conceptions and acquainting the reader with unique patterns amid the predominant facts. Reviews assemble, evaluate, analyze, and combine the available facts or data on any subject, according to Bahishti [25].

The information has been gathered using a variety of search engines, databases, and websites. Google Scholar, PubMed, Science Direct, ProQuest, and renowned and publicly available articles from a few reliable and pertinent journals in media and AI are the main research sources. Additionally, combinations of pertinent keywords were employed to find the needed content, for example, “AI-generated content,” “copyright issues and protection,” “originality,” “creativity,” “law,” and the perspective of “different media and professional practitioners considering the AI-assisted content.” Moreover, the study has conducted the inclusion and exclusion criteria to further strengthen article selection from the literature: the paper or review should be written in the English language, articles related to AI-generated media and copyright protection will be included, and most papers are from 2017 to present to ensure that the information is relevant. Articles that mostly concentrated on journalism's basic functions, or significantly departed from the issue, were not included in the review.

Originality

Originality is the most important factor to take into account when determining a work's eligibility for copyright protection [26]. According to Margoni, only works that exhibit a certain level of originality are eligible for protection under copyright law [27]. Consequently, uniqueness frequently plays a vital part in the ownership of the work, not just in the case of AI-assisted material or content.

The question of whether AI-assisted media output counts as an “authorship original work” has also been the subject of numerous discussions [28]. Some scholars [29, 30] looked at the authorship standards and guidelines to examine and compare how much they apply to work produced by AI-assisted content.

However, Lemley [31] mentioned that the concept of originality is complex in the context of AI, as content is often generated by learning from large datasets of existing human-created works. Bulayenko et al. [32] further added that AI could produce novel combinations and variations, but whether interchangeable AI-generated content meets the threshold of human creativity remains a topic of debate.

Moreover, different states have different conceptions of what uniqueness or originality is and how it is defined. For instance, originality is the primary need for something to be labeled “work” and, as a result, is eligible for legal rights, notwithstanding the protection of copyright and controversy for AI-generated media in China [24]. The emphasis on individuality comes from a different angle in other nations like the United Kingdom (UK) and Hong Kong. It is primarily concerned with the content being created by an author by using the appropriate abilities, efforts, or labor and not by using copy-and-paste techniques [33]. In contrast, a few later occurrences have caused the European Union (EU) to advance. It has been said that the necessity of being the author's own “intellectual property or creation” and not only the author's skills or efforts has been brought forth [24].

Murray [34] mentioned that the agreement of trade and cooperation between the EU and the UK shapes these international standards, such as the Berne Convention, and preserves high copyright protection standards between the EU and UK. Furthermore, the United States’ (US) perspective and standards, on the other hand, appear to be somewhere in the middle of the previous ones, as they require that the work be original and involve at minimum creativity, which is referred to as a creative “spark” and “modicum” [35].

Ramirez Caminatti [36] stressed that Canada's Copyright Act safeguards original works. The act doesn’t explicitly mention interchangeable content, leaving the application of copyright law to such content a matter of legal interpretation. Courts would likely assess the level of human involvement and creativity in AI-generated work. However, Japan's Copyright Act protects original literary and artistic works. Similarly, Australian copyright law guards original literary, dramatic, musical, and creative works. The Copyright Act doesn’t distinguish between works created by humans or AI. Kucukali [37] notes that protection is decided based on the originality and creativity exhibited in the content. For instance, Hutson and Harper-Nichols [38] stated that in Japan, a musician uses AI software to compose a piece of music that combines elements from various traditional Japanese folk songs. AI generates a new melody inspired by these folk songs but is distinct from any source. The musician releases the composition as a single, gaining attention on streaming platforms. However, a folk music preservation society claims that AI-generated music borrows too heavily from their cultural heritage and violates their rights to traditional tunes.

Likewise, in the case of India, Chaudhary and Vries [39] mention that a filmmaker employs AI algorithms to generate scenes, characters, and dialogues for a feature film. The AI algorithm takes inspiration from popular Bollywood movies but produces a unique storyline and visuals. The film is released and becomes a box office hit. However, a production company accuses the filmmaker of copyright infringement, arguing that the AI's output reproduces substantial elements of their movies without permission. The case tests the limits of derivative works in the context of AI-assisted generated content.

In all these jurisdictions, the central principle is that copyright protection extends to original creative works, regardless of whether humans or AI creates them. The challenge lies in adapting existing copyright frameworks to accommodate the unique characteristics of interchangeable content and determining how copyright law should apply to such works.

Thence, diverse explanations for what is expected to be regarded as original work and what requires legal protection were provided by different perspectives, requirements, and lookouts for originality.

Creativity

Creativity is another critical aspect relating to copyright protection in the case of AI-generated content. Several scholars [40, 41] have highlighted and demonstrated that copyright law has historically focused on protecting works created by human creators. This is due to the belief that human creativity involves conscious choices, emotions, and intentions that machines cannot replicate. Traditional copyright criteria, such as the requirement for a “human author,” reflect this perspective. However, as AI technologies advance, the line between human-generated and machine-generated creativity becomes increasingly unclear [42]. Though, there are still instances where the artists have disputed this idea and tried to disprove it. For instance, Jason M. Allen's painting “Théâtre d’Opéra Spatial” is a well-known illustration of this. In 2022, Allen entered the photo at the Colorado State Fair and took home the top honor [43]. However, the revelation that the image was produced by the AI program “Midjourney” sparked significant controversy and negative reactions [44]. On the contrary, other artists alleged that he had not played fairly and that the use of AI had diminished the quality of their creations. Additionally, Erdine [45] added that some claim that AI software and algorithms constitute a “high-tech version of plagiarism.” Allen, however, remained unapologetic in the face of the negative effects, welcomed the criticism, and further revealed that he had disclosed that the artwork had been made with the aid of artificial intelligence [46].

Additionally, he declared, “You said AI would never be as good as you, that AI would never do the work you do, and I said, ‘Oh really?’” indicating to other artists, and “Allen referred to the winning prize on this.” It actually did happen that an AI-assisted created piece of art took home the top honor in a competition [47]. Another comparable but distinct instance occurred when German artist Boris Eldagsen won the Sony World Photography Award for his entry named “The Electrician,” but declined to accept it since, as he later claimed, it was an AI-assisted work of art [48]. Artistic interpretation: “AI is not photography. As a result, I decline the honour” [49].

The two discussed instances have demonstrated how different artists view AI-generated content, not only in the context of visual arts but also in the creation of other media content. Thence, it can be said that some artists consider AI to be a component of innovation and creativity. On the other hand, others view it as only a high-tech algorithm and a facilitator of creativity, but not as creativity itself. According to Bieser [50], AI has the power to inspire the creativity of humans through assisting in the creation of content. Even yet, it cannot be deemed creative because it cannot inherently produce fresh ideas. Thus, in light of the current situation, the subject of copyright is once more raised because it is thought that copyright protection is meant to encourage creative activities and expressions [51]. As a result, there are many ways to define and view creativity, and different viewpoints on copyright defilements.

Legal Aspects

As was previously mentioned, “Dream Writer” received legal permission to use the copyright for one of its articles in China in 2019 [17, 19]. This was the first instance of copyright protection for AI-generated media. The existence of a legal infrastructure for promoting those breakthroughs is crucial since China wants to become a “global AI innovation hub” by 2030 [18, 52]; as a result, China has addressed the copyright issue for content produced with the assistance of AI in great detail and has granted the necessary legal protections to both the organizations that create the work as well as the AI itself. Volpicelli [44] highlighted that in the case of other nations, including the EU and the US, the officials generally concur that if a person participates in the creation of any “AI-assisted artwork,” he or she has the right to that work. To regulate the rapidly developing AI technologies, the European Commission also began formulating an AI Act about two years ago. As a result, it attracted significant attention and gained more investments [53], which was directly followed by the introduction of ChatGPT.

Mukherjee et al. [53] stressed that companies that utilize AI algorithms and tools for the creation of content or media will be required to report any copyrighted materials used in the development of their systems per a prior EU agreement. A list of interpretive factors for determining the originality of a work has been put out by the Court of Justice of the EU. According to the established criteria, a piece of work is deemed original when the author is able to make “free and creative choices” and infuse their “personal stamp” into it, Margoni [27] added.

Despite the fact that the Berne Convention for the Protection of Artistic and Literary and Works, which was adopted in 1886 by ten EU nations [54], lacks a clear definition for the “author” of a work, the script and its historical context strongly sponsor that the references to “authorship” and “author” in the Convention chiefly infer a natural person who formed the effort, labor, or work that proposes that the originality of copyright protection devolves in “human authors” [28].

Mathur [22] highlighted that as an alternative to the Berne Convention, in 1952, UNESCO formulated the Universal Copyright Convention (UCC). The UCC was intended to cater to the copyright protection needs of various nations, including the Soviet Union and the United States, who desired some level of multilateral protection without becoming part of the Berne Convention. Compared to regulations of the Berne Convention, the UCC's rules are more adaptable. That adaptability accommodated countries in varying developmental stages and with diverse social and economic systems. Like the Berne Convention, the UCC upholds the principle of national treatment and condemns discrimination against foreign authors. However, it imposes fewer mandatory requirements on member nations [55]. Relating to the copyright laws in the EU, the criteria of existing EU copyright regulations are mostly practical and rather flexible in dealing with the difficulties of output generated by AI-assisted technology [28, 37].

Likewise, Sganga [56] addressed that EU's copyright directive article 17, also known as the “Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market,” forbids platforms that share content from exhibiting copyrighted material without proper licenses for their users. In June 2017, this law was adopted by the EU, and from the mentioned date, member states were required to put it into effect [32]. Bird, Ungless, and Kasirzadeh [57] cited that safeguarding copyright for published works in the UK extends up to seventy years following the author's demise. Nevertheless, the duration of copyright varies based on the nature of the work and its publication status. Once the copyright term concludes, the work enters the public domain.

However, in Switzerland, the duration of copyright protection is determined by specific timelines depending on the type [58]. For creative works, copyright coverage concludes seventy years following the author's death, while for computer programs, it extends for fifty years. In the case of photographs lacking distinct individuality, their copyright safeguard ends fifty years after the moment of their creation [59]. These regulations in Switzerland govern copyright protection for various types of intellectual designs that ensure a balance between encouraging creativity and eventually making works available for public use.

As the definitions and descriptions greatly vary among nations and laws, there is no generally accepted definition of originality and the authors’ contribution criteria that can be used to explain the aspects of copyright law in different legislations.

Media Practitioners’ and Related Professionals’ Opinions on AI-Generated Content

The attitudes of media professionals, including broadcasters, reporters, journalists, stakeholders, and others toward the issues of originality, creativity, and legality regarding copyright also differ dramatically in this paradigm. Some people contend that content produced by AI has given this market a new life, whereas others are skeptical and worried that this invention will push human creators to the side and eventually substitute them, especially now that AI has the necessary copyright protection [60]. Consequently, study researchers have examined this field by integrating the perceptions of media practitioners.

Media Practitioner's Perception Regarding AI-Generated Content

In order to better understand their perceptions of the way they expect AI to impact their employment, the media workforce, and how journalists understand their adaptability and resilience, Yuand Huang [61] conducted a study in which they conducted in-depth interviews and engaged media practitioners from the media industry of China. Their research revealed that, in contrast to those from smaller organizations, journalists from larger media organizations tended to favor the use of AI in their industry. The authors described this as a “dynamic interplay amid personal and situational attributes” and noted that, generally, their respondents tended to see the AI integration with human labor favorably.

Franceschelli and Musolesi [62] added that media practitioners view AI as an experimental tool that allows them to explore new creative avenues. They are excited about using AI to generate unique content that pushes boundaries and challenges traditional norms. However, AI-generated content lacks the human touch and creativity of human-driven efforts and can create problems, including repetitive content, that compromise the uniqueness and authenticity of media practitioners’ work. These new works themselves might be difficult or impossible to copyright, causing issues in the future; the NYU Journal of Copyright and Entertainment Law discussed the difficulty that one can have copyrighting work where AI was involved at all as an end-product. In the D.C. Circuit decision Thaler v. Perlmutter, the plaintiff Stephen Thaler applied for copyright for a visual piece he created with a “proprietary AI platform” he developed that he calls the “Creativity Machine.” When he applied for the copyright, he listed the “author” as the Creativity Machine, but himself as the owner. “According to Thaler, he had no direct involvement in the creation of the artwork bar the prompt he gave” [63]. The Copyright Office denied his copyright claim, adding clarification in the appeal that “for the reasons explained below, defendants are correct that human authorship is an essential part of a valid copyright claim, and therefore plaintiff's pending motion for summary judgment is denied and defendants’ pending cross-motion for summary judgment is granted” [64].

Lu et al. [65] continued research in this area by examining how people view photos produced by AI. The scientists warned about the risks posed by AI-generated media and stated that it is impossible for people to tell an AI-generated image from a real one. Zhang and Gosline [66] conducted a study examining how people view AI-generated content by having participants rate the quality of content created through four different AI-human collaboration methods. The study found that participants’ perceptions of AI-assisted media were influenced by their biases. When unaware that AI was involved, participants rated the content highly. However, once they learned humans were also part of the process, they showed a preference for human-assisted content, a phenomenon termed “human favoritism.”

From the preceding discussion, media practitioners’ perceptions of AI-generated content can vary widely, ranging from enthusiasm for its innovative potential to concerns relating to authenticity and ethical implications. As AI technology evolves, these perceptions will be expected to shift and adapt alongside it [67, 68].

Perception of Professionals Regarding AI-Generated Content

Vimpari et al. [69] presented a comprehensive summary of how professionals perceive AI-created media, specifically focusing on images, and found that legal professionals have concerns about copyright ownership and the legal implications of AI-generated content, but there is a chance to navigate complex intellectual property issues and ensure that AI-assisted generated works comply with copyright laws [70].

Tiwary [20] conducted a study to investigate how academics view the utilization of AI tools like ChatGPT for generating content. The results indicated that these professionals believed AI tools were beneficial in enhancing their sentence construction, language usage, and content creation process. However, they also emphasized that AI tools had limited accuracy. Therefore, they suggested verifying the AI-generated content and utilizing it to improve writing while avoiding complete plagiarism. Likewise, professionals in academia stress the importance of transparency in AI-generated research and the need to follow ethical standards that guarantee that AI tools are used responsibly. In his research, Mezei [71] contended that attributing copyright to AI-generated content is inadequate and unrealistic due to its inability to address evolving perspectives. He asserted that copyright law is a fabricated construct, representing a legal embodiment of intricate, ever-changing sociocultural and economic interests. Additionally, Fernandez [41] highlighted that journalists and content creators often value AI for its ability to process and analyze large amounts of data quickly. AI can help with fact-checking, analysis of data, and summarizing information.

From the perceptions of professionals, it can be found that their perceptions of AI-assisted content generated vary based on their industry, role, and personal experiences. Although some embrace AI as an innovative tool that enhances efficiency and creativity, on the other hand, others express concerns such as issues like authenticity, bias, ethics, and copyright.

Ethical Consideration Related to AI-Generated Content

The ethical concerns associated with AI-generated content are not limited to copyright issues or its encroachment into various media domains. There is the difficulty of detecting AI involvement, especially in nonprofessional and smaller-scale settings like education [72]. Students’ utilization of AI tools for content creation in these contexts raises ethical questions. Uzun and Levent [73] engaged in a discussion about integrating AI tools and upholding academic integrity within this framework. The researchers suggested the use of detection tools to identify manipulated content due to AI's widespread impact across diverse domains. They argued that in the current AI era, discerning whether the content is human or AI-generated might not be productive, implying the need for a nuanced approach to address AI-generated content's challenges.

Summarizing the collection of studies discussed earlier, these studies reveal that practitioners’ viewpoints differ across fields, and individual preferences and favoritism play a significant role in shaping these perceptions. Undoubtedly, AI-generated content provides novelty, efficiency, and productivity, and less time is required to get help or support from AI tools to generate the content.

However, it also possesses some concerns or risks attached to it, for example, reliance on AI-assisted content might lead to a perceived loss of authenticity and human emotional connection relating to creative works. Vallis et al. [74] said that the fine line between inspiration and plagiarism becomes blurrier with the capacity of AI to impersonate present works in such a way that can potentially sidestep copyright protections. Moreover, while discussing the risks of AI-generated content, Bran et al. [75] added that the automation of content creation tends to cause job displacement in creative industries, affecting artists, writers, and related professionals. Additionally, interchangeable or AI-assisted content can be used to create deepfakes, misinformation, and malicious content, which raises concerns about spreading fake news and the attrition of truth.

Recommendation for Viable Copyright Flows for the Future

Some possible ways forward for copyright concerns are beginning to be shared, particularly in images and video. Adobe Firefly, which provides generative AI for the Adobe Creative Suite of software, including Photoshop, Illustrator, Substance, Stager, and more, which creates 2D and 3D images and vectors, presents some possible solutions. Released in 2023, Firefly is, according to Adobe, “Trained on Adobe Stock images, openly licensed content, and public domain content.” Therefore, they claim it is “safe for commercial use.” In addition, they claim to have created a “compensation model for Adobe Stock contributors whose content is used in the dataset to retrain Firefly models” [76].

The Content Authenticity Initiative (CAI) is about 1,200 entities, “a community of media and tech companies, NGOs, academics, and others working to promote adoption of an open industry standard for content authenticity and provenance” [77]. Founded in 2019, the CAI, in their 2021 white paper, describes their work as pursuing three main goals. First, a “detection of deliberately deceptive media” [78]. They note that people with bad intentions may use technology that moves as fast or faster than detection, a type of arms race, like the new AI detection tools offered by the company Turn-it-in, alongside its traditional academic plagiarism detection tools.

Second, they note, “education is essential.” They urge media literacy campaigns and institutional education. “Finally, we must consider content attribution … often referred to as provenance, attribution empowers content creators and editors, regardless of their geographic location or degree of access to technology, to disclose information about who created or changed an asset, what was changed, and how it was changed” [78].

Opening the computer software “terminal” area, one can see the history of the creation of the images and assets. In addition to this comprehensive image history, the CAI would also promote tools that make it easier for creators to declare their use of AI at the point of upload.

In 2021, Adobe co-founded the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity (C2PA) standards organization, along with Microsoft, Truepic, Arm, Intel, and the BBC. In collaboration with Microsoft and BBC-backed Project Origin, they have the stated aim of enabling “cryptographically verifiable facts about content to engender trust across all the surfaces through which we consume content” [78].

Their white paper considers individuals and not just institutions. They give an example in which a human rights activist, acting alone, may record something with an NGO-provided application such as “Proof mode,” or, they outline, they can select their user settings and preferences within the tool before capturing in the case of using the native video or photo recording of their phone or apps, which would have to adopt this system. Their goal would be that “if the user is not connected to an organization, it is likely that the asset will be later discovered by an NGO or media outlet on messaging and social platforms. These institutions will be able to read the associated CAI data and confirm key attribution aspects before verifying that the asset is accurate” [78].

They go on to propose that the NGOs and media outlets would then begin their own verification process, likely looking at information such as author, time, location, etc. They note that if the asset has preserved CAI data, it will significantly simplify this process. The institution will then likely try to contact the source as part of the verification and may or may not receive the details they desire to feel comfortable sharing on their platform. (If required, this would also be where an institution may decide to use redaction capabilities, for example, blurring out faces before distributing widely.) Assuming the verification process is completed, in a media context, the workflow is then in the hands of a photo editor who will complete a similar process as the required photojournalism protocols to post the asset. They note that empowers the source, and not simply the outlet, to be the trusted entity. “As consumers view the content on social media platforms and/or the CAI website, the attribution details that they can see will start with the original capture and mitigate uncertainty for end users who may or may not trust the publishing institution.” [78]

Adobe added that they were planning and working toward a “universal ‘Do Not Train’ Content Credentials tag that will remain associated with a piece of content wherever it's used, published, or stored.” [76]

Limitations

However, the recommended strategies have limitations that media practitioners can face while implementing, including,

  • AI-assisted generated content may not consistently meet the desired quality standards, leading to output quality variations. To address this issue, media practitioners need to ensure consistent and high-quality content that can require manual oversight and intervention.

  • Using AI to replicate human voices, faces, or styles can raise ethical concerns about consent, privacy, and misrepresentation. Practitioners need to ensure that AI-generated content aligns with ethical standards.

  • It can be complex to determine the copyright ownership of AI-generated content.

  • AI algorithms can unintentionally maintain biases present in training data. To mitigate those biases, practitioners must actively address potential biases in AI-generated content, particularly in language, image recognition, and content recommendations.

  • Implementing interchangeable AI-generated content might necessitate investment in resources, including hardware, software, and skilled personnel capable of effectively understanding and managing AI tools.

  • The effectiveness of AI-assisted-generated content relies on the quality and diversity of the training data. If the training data is inadequate or unrepresentative, the AI output may not be accurate or relevant.

  • The legal and regulatory landscape surrounding AI-generated content is still evolving. Practitioners must stay informed about copyright laws, intellectual property rights, and potential liabilities.

CONCLUSION

AI-assisted-generated content is an evolving and complex topic encompassing various industries and roles. Nevertheless, as the landscape keeps evolving and significant advancements are made, concerns surrounding originality, copyright, and the conventional ownership of AI-generated content have emerged as pressing issues. To address the indicated notion, the current study has observed the case of copyright protection in interchangeable content concerning originality, creativity, and law. To achieve this study`s objectives or aims, the study followed a review methodology and analysis of the existing body of literature to gain an inclusive understanding of the present perspective regarding copyright challenges related to AI-generated media content. Likewise, the study has demonstrated the viewpoints of stakeholders such as media practitioners and professionals to gain better and more practical insights into AI-generated content.

From the current research, the notions of originality, creativity, and legal aspects are closely intertwined and complex when examined within the context of copyright in AI-assisted content.

The analysis of recent studies on this topic clearly reveals a wide spectrum of viewpoints and criticisms. These perspectives differ significantly across nations, researchers, journalists, and other relevant stakeholders, often shaped by individual subjective beliefs and, at times, grounded in objective arguments. However, a consistent theme emerges: the copyright protection afforded to AI-generated content is expected to be a pivotal concern for the future of human creators. This issue poses several potential risks for both the prospects of human-authored content and the broader landscape of content generation.

Furthermore, the research offers suggestions and highlights associated limitations for the implementation of these proposed ideas. In this context, researchers could consider conducting a comprehensive cross-country analysis of copyright laws, specifically focusing on AI-generated content. This approach could shed light on the current situation within this domain, offering a transparent and comprehensive portrayal of the complex landscape.

12Innovative Applications of AI for Sustainable Supply Chain Management in Environmental Conservation

Saydulu Kolasani

DOI: 10.1201/9781003497189-12

INTRODUCTION

The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into sustainable supply chain management represents a significant advancement in environmental conservation efforts. In recent years, the intersection of AI and sustainability has garnered increasing attention as organizations seek innovative solutions to minimize environmental impact while maintaining operational efficiency in their supply chain processes. This introduction provides an overview of the key concepts, challenges, and opportunities associated with the application of AI in sustainable supply chain management for environmental conservation.

Background

Supply chain management encompasses the coordination of activities involved in sourcing, production, transportation, and distribution to deliver products or services to end customers. Traditional supply chain practices often prioritize cost reduction and operational efficiency, sometimes at the expense of environmental sustainability. However, the growing recognition of the environmental and social impacts associated with supply chain operations has prompted organizations to adopt more sustainable practices.

Environmental conservation is a critical component of sustainability, focusing on the preservation and protection of natural resources, ecosystems, and biodiversity. Achieving environmental conservation goals requires minimizing resource consumption, reducing pollution, and mitigating the negative impacts of human activities on the environment. Sustainable supply chain management plays a vital role in advancing environmental conservation objectives by optimizing resource utilization, minimizing waste, and adopting eco-friendly practices throughout the supply chain.

The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Sustainable Supply Chain Management

Artificial intelligence, encompassing machine learning, natural language processing, and other advanced technologies, has emerged as a powerful tool for optimizing supply chain processes and driving sustainability initiatives. AI enables organizations to analyze vast amounts of data, identify patterns and trends, and make data-driven decisions to improve efficiency and reduce environmental impact across the supply chain.

Predictive analytics is one of the key applications of AI in sustainable supply chain management. By leveraging historical data and machine learning algorithms, organizations can forecast demand more accurately, optimize inventory levels, and minimize stockouts and excess inventory. This proactive approach to demand forecasting helps reduce waste, lower inventory holding costs, and enhance resource efficiency.

Another area where AI is making significant contributions to sustainable supply chain management is logistics optimization. AI-powered algorithms can optimize transportation routes, mode selection, and vehicle scheduling to minimize fuel consumption, reduce emissions, and lower transportation costs. By considering factors such as delivery time windows, traffic conditions, and vehicle capacities, AI-based logistics optimization systems improve delivery efficiency while reducing the carbon footprint of transportation operations. Furthermore, AI technologies are being deployed for real-time monitoring and management of environmental performance in supply chain operations. Internet of Things (IoT) devices, equipped with sensors and connectivity capabilities, collect data on energy usage, emissions, and environmental conditions in manufacturing facilities, warehouses, and transportation vehicles. AI algorithms analyze this data in real time to identify inefficiencies, detect anomalies, and recommend corrective actions to optimize resource utilization and minimize environmental impact.

Challenges and Opportunities

While the adoption of AI in sustainable supply chain management offers numerous benefits, it also presents challenges and considerations that must be addressed. One of the primary challenges is data quality and availability. AI models rely on large volumes of high-quality data to deliver accurate predictions and recommendations. However, supply chain data is often fragmented, inconsistent, and of varying quality, making it challenging to train AI models effectively.

Another challenge is the integration of AI technologies into existing supply chain systems and processes. Organizations may face resistance to change, technical barriers, and interoperability issues when implementing AI solutions. Additionally, concerns related to data privacy, security, and ethical use of AI pose significant considerations that must be addressed to ensure responsible deployment and adoption of AI in supply chain management.

Despite these challenges, the integration of AI in sustainable supply chain management offers significant opportunities for environmental conservation and sustainability. AI-driven optimization algorithms can help organizations achieve cost savings, enhance operational efficiency, and reduce environmental impact simultaneously. Furthermore, AI technologies enable real-time monitoring and decision-making, allowing organizations to respond proactively to environmental risks and opportunities in the supply chain.

The integration of artificial intelligence in sustainable supply chain management holds immense potential for advancing environmental conservation objectives. By leveraging AI technologies to optimize supply chain processes, organizations can achieve operational efficiency gains while minimizing environmental impact throughout the value chain. However, addressing challenges related to data quality, integration, and ethical considerations is essential to ensure the responsible deployment and adoption of AI in supply chain management for environmental conservation. In the subsequent chapters of this book, we will explore in detail the innovative applications, case studies, and best practices of AI in sustainable supply chain management for environmental conservation.

LITERATURE REVIEW

The integration of AI in sustainable supply chain management has gained increasing attention from researchers and practitioners seeking innovative solutions to address environmental challenges while maintaining operational efficiency. This literature review provides a comprehensive overview of existing research and developments in the application of AI technologies for environmental conservation within supply chain operations.

AI Applications in Sustainable Supply Chain Management

AI technologies, including machine learning, natural language processing, and predictive analytics, offer a range of applications for optimizing supply chain processes and driving sustainability initiatives. One of the primary applications of AI in sustainable supply chain management is demand forecasting and inventory optimization. By analyzing historical sales data and external factors such as weather patterns and economic indicators, AI-powered forecasting models can generate accurate predictions of future demand, allowing organizations to optimize inventory levels, minimize stockouts, and reduce waste (Gunasekaran et al., 2018).

Another area where AI is making significant contributions is logistics optimization. AI-driven algorithms can optimize transportation routes, mode selection, and vehicle scheduling to minimize fuel consumption, reduce emissions, and lower transportation costs. By considering factors such as delivery time windows, traffic conditions, and vehicle capacities, AI-based logistics optimization systems improve delivery efficiency while reducing the carbon footprint of transportation operations (Deng et al., 2018). Furthermore, AI technologies enable real-time monitoring and management of environmental performance in supply chain operations. Internet of Things (IoT) devices equipped with sensors and connectivity capabilities collect data on energy usage, emissions, and environmental conditions in manufacturing facilities, warehouses, and transportation vehicles. AI algorithms analyze this data in real time to identify inefficiencies, detect anomalies, and recommend corrective actions to optimize resource utilization and minimize environmental impact (Cheng et al., 2020).

In recent years, significant advancements in technology have transformed various fields, addressing both environmental and data management challenges. Chen and Zhang (2018) review the application of big data technology in pollution control, highlighting its role in tackling environmental issues through data-driven approaches. Complementing this, Duan et al. (2019) provide an overview of blockchain technology from a big data perspective, emphasizing its potential in enhancing data security and integrity. In the realm of financial forecasting, Hsu and Kao (2018) explore the use of deep learning for stock price prediction, illustrating the impact of advanced algorithms on market analysis. Jia and Zhang (2018) discuss a blockchain-based framework for ensuring data integrity in IoT applications, reflecting the growing intersection between blockchain and IoT technologies. Kong et al. (2020) introduce the concept of “Big Earth” data, marking a new frontier in Earth and information sciences, while Li and Liu (2020) review the role of artificial intelligence in achieving sustainable development goals, underscoring its importance in driving global sustainability efforts. Robinson and Barr (2017) critically appraise deep learning, providing insights into its capabilities and limitations. Wang et al. (2019) examine the use of big data analytics in knowledge management, revealing its influence on organizational learning and decision-making. Wu et al. (2020) offer a comprehensive review of digital twin technology, highlighting its potential from a knowledge perspective. Xiao and Tao (2017) focus on the design and implementation of an IoT-based green logistics system, demonstrating how IoT can contribute to sustainable logistics. Lastly, Yang and McCollister (2017) explore the effects of artificial intelligence on human beings, shedding light on its broader implications. Zhang et al. (2018) emphasize the role of big data in sustainable development, framing it as a critical tool for addressing global challenges. Collectively, these studies illustrate the transformative impact of emerging technologies on various sectors, from environmental management and data integrity to financial forecasting and sustainability.

Challenges and Considerations

Despite the potential benefits of AI in sustainable supply chain management, several challenges and considerations must be addressed to ensure successful implementation and adoption. Data quality and availability emerge as significant challenges, as AI models rely on large volumes of high-quality data to deliver accurate predictions and recommendations. Supply chain data is often fragmented, inconsistent, and of varying quality, making it challenging to train AI models effectively (Wamba et al., 2017).

Additionally, the integration of AI technologies into existing supply chain systems and processes poses technical and organizational challenges. Organizations may encounter resistance to change, technical barriers, and interoperability issues when implementing AI solutions. Furthermore, concerns related to data privacy, security, and ethical use of AI raise important considerations that must be addressed to ensure responsible deployment and adoption of AI in supply chain management (Govindan et al., 2020).

Research Directions and Future Trends

Looking ahead, several research directions and future trends emerge in the application of AI for environmental conservation within supply chain operations. One area of focus is the development of AI-powered decision support systems that enable organizations to make informed, data-driven decisions to optimize supply chain processes and minimize environmental impact. Additionally, research efforts are needed to explore the potential of emerging AI technologies such as deep learning and reinforcement learning in addressing complex sustainability challenges in supply chain management (Triguero et al., 2018).

There is a growing need for interdisciplinary research collaborations among academia, industry, and government agencies to develop holistic approaches to sustainable supply chain management. Collaboration across disciplines such as engineering, environmental science, economics, and information technology is essential to address the multifaceted challenges of environmental conservation within supply chain operations. Additionally, research on policy interventions, regulatory frameworks, and incentives to promote the adoption of AI technologies for sustainability in supply chains can help drive meaningful change at the organizational and systemic levels (Wu et al., 2020).

The literature on the integration of artificial intelligence in sustainable supply chain management highlights the transformative potential of AI technologies to drive environmental conservation initiatives within supply chain operations. By leveraging AI for demand forecasting, inventory optimization, logistics optimization, and environmental monitoring, organizations can achieve operational efficiency gains while minimizing environmental impact throughout the value chain. However, addressing challenges related to data quality, integration, and ethical considerations is essential to ensure the responsible deployment and adoption of AI in supply chain management for environmental conservation. Future research efforts should focus on developing innovative AI-powered solutions, fostering interdisciplinary collaborations, and advancing policy initiatives to promote sustainability in supply chains.

INNOVATIVE APPLICATIONS OF AI FOR ENVIRONMENTAL CONSERVATION

Demand Forecasting and Inventory Optimization

Demand forecasting and inventory optimization are critical aspects of sustainable supply chain management. By accurately predicting demand and optimizing inventory levels, organizations can minimize waste, reduce resource consumption, and lower environmental impact. AI technologies play a crucial role in enhancing demand forecasting and inventory optimization processes.

AI-powered demand forecasting models leverage historical sales data, market trends, and external factors such as weather patterns and economic indicators to generate accurate predictions of future demand. These models use advanced machine learning algorithms to analyze large datasets and identify patterns and trends that traditional forecasting methods may overlook. By improving the accuracy of demand forecasts, AI enables organizations to optimize inventory levels, minimize stockouts and excess inventory, and reduce waste throughout the supply chain. AI-driven inventory optimization systems continuously monitor inventory levels, demand patterns, and supply chain dynamics to dynamically adjust stocking levels and reorder points. These systems use real-time data and predictive analytics to optimize inventory replenishment decisions, ensuring that the right products are available at the right time and minimizing the environmental impact of excess inventory and overstocking.

Logistics Optimization

Logistics optimization is another area where AI technologies can contribute to environmental conservation efforts. Transportation and logistics operations account for a significant portion of greenhouse gas emissions and environmental impact in supply chains. By optimizing transportation routes, mode selection, and vehicle scheduling, organizations can reduce fuel consumption, lower emissions, and minimize the carbon footprint of logistics operations.

AI-powered logistics optimization systems leverage algorithms such as genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, and reinforcement learning to find the most efficient routes and schedules for transporting goods. These systems consider factors such as delivery time windows, traffic conditions, vehicle capacities, and fuel efficiency to optimize transportation plans and minimize environmental impact. By incorporating real-time data and predictive analytics, AI-driven logistics optimization systems can dynamically adjust routes and schedules in response to changing conditions, further enhancing efficiency and reducing environmental impact.

Real-Time Environmental Monitoring

Real-time environmental monitoring is essential for identifying and mitigating environmental risks and impacts associated with supply chain operations. By continuously monitoring environmental conditions such as air quality, water quality, and noise levels, organizations can detect anomalies, identify potential environmental hazards, and take proactive measures to minimize their impact on ecosystems and communities.

AI technologies, combined with IoT devices and sensor networks, enable real-time environmental monitoring systems that collect, analyze, and visualize environmental data in real time. Machine learning algorithms process sensor data and identify patterns, trends, and anomalies indicative of environmental risks or impacts. These systems provide organizations with actionable insights and alerts, enabling them to respond quickly to environmental incidents, implement corrective actions, and mitigate potential environmental damage. Demand forecasting and inventory optimization, logistics optimization, and real-time environmental monitoring are innovative applications of AI that contribute to environmental conservation efforts within supply chain operations. By leveraging AI technologies to optimize supply chain processes, organizations can minimize waste, reduce resource consumption, and lower environmental impact throughout the value chain.
